"My dearest wish," keeper Fettle had written, "is that one day a child will come who cares enough to keep the animals alive after I am gone. Someone who sees them not as toys but as friends. That child, whoever they are, will have the whole of my heart's work as their gift." Nia closed the journal gently. She sat for a moment in the warm lamp light. Now she understood everything.

{~HERO:Nia~} closed keeper Fettle's private journal. She understood everything now. The zoo was not just a set of clockwork animals. It was one old man's life poured into brass and tin. His great hope was simply that a child like her might come along and care. Before she left the shop, {~HERO:Nia~} found a blank page at the back of the journal. She wrote a note. She promised to come back, to help, to learn. When keeper Fettle returned and found the note, he knew his life's work was safe. And {~HERO:Nia~}, walking home through the morning streets with Tock on her shoulder, carried a new purpose in her heart.

A second clockwork mouse kept darting out from behind the board. It was twin to Tock in every way. Same brass paws. Same whirring tail. It would look back at {~HERO:Nia~} and then vanish again. It clearly wanted her to follow. But the way it led was into a dark gap behind the workbench. It was a narrow space full of dust and webs. {~HERO:Nia~} could chase after it into the dark, crawling on her hands and knees. Or she could coax it to come to her, using Tock as a lure. Tock, for his part, seemed drawn to his twin.

choices.label: Chase the mouse into the dark.
Coax the mouse gently to you.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Nia~} crouched down and crawled after the second mouse. Tock rode on her back. The space behind the board was tight and dusty. But after a few feet it opened into a tiny hidden room. It was no larger than a cupboard. Inside, a hidden nest of clockwork mice slept in a pile of felt scraps. There were a dozen of them, all different sizes. Their brass bodies gleamed in the light of {~HERO:Nia~}'s candle stub. This was keeper Fettle's secret. He had built a whole family of clockwork mice for company. The twin mouse hopped into the nest. It looked up at {~HERO:Nia~} as if waiting.

{~HERO:Nia~} wound them one by one. Each tiny clockwork mouse. Soon a dozen of them ran out into the shop. They ran in happy circles around Tock. He sat up tall, now the leader of a whole brass family. When keeper Fettle returned, he was full of joy. Someone had found his small friends. He was even more overjoyed to see Tock with a dozen new siblings. "Every keeper needs helpers," he said. From that day on, the clockwork mice cared for the museum with him. {~HERO:Nia~} visited often. When she did, a chorus of tiny squeaks would greet her at the door.

The second clockwork mouse would not be caught. It just sat in the gap behind the board. Its whiskers twitched. It watched {~HERO:Nia~} with bright glass eyes. It let her come close, but not touch. All through the last hour of the night, it kept her company. It was a patient friend in the dark shop. {~HERO:Nia~} never did learn just where it wanted to lead her. But she was not alone. When dawn broke and the keepers came, the twin mouse slipped away into its hidden nest. {~HERO:Nia~} walked out into the morning with Tock on her shoulder. She was content that some mysteries were best left unsolved.

The one locked cabinet in the shop was old and lovely. Its wood was dark with age. Its brass lock was shaped like a tiny gear. {~HERO:Nia~} felt sure it held keeper Fettle's greatest secret. The question was how to open it. The tiny keys on the master ring she had taken from the clock's hook might fit. She just had to try each one. Or, there was a strong driver in the keeper tool box. With enough force, she could maybe pry the lock open. But forcing old things, she had learned, rarely ended well.

choices.label: Try the tiny keys on the master ring one by one.
Force the lock with a tool.

nodes.body: Patiently, {~HERO:Nia~} tried the tiny keys on the master ring one by one. The first was too big. The second turned but didn't catch. The third, fourth, and fifth were all wrong shapes. Tock sat beside her, watching the process with intense concentration, as if he understood the importance of finding the right one. The sixth key—a small, simple brass key with a clover-shaped bow—slid into the lock and turned with a soft click. The cabinet's door swung open on silent hinges. {~HERO:Nia~} held her breath.

Inside the cabinet, on a soft cushion, sat a small worn brass rabbit. It was older than all the other animals Nia had seen. Its brass was dulled to a deep brown. Its ears were chipped at the edges. Its little paws were worn smooth from years of handling. A note in a faded envelope was tucked beside it. "My first. Always keep it safe." Nia lifted the rabbit gently. She felt its weight. She saw the tiny keyhole under its chin. This was where the whole zoo began, a lifetime ago.

{~HERO:Nia~} wound the small worn brass rabbit with the greatest care, and it hopped slowly, faithfully, across the workshop floor. Thump... thump... thump went its little tin feet, as they must have a lifetime ago when keeper Fettle first set it moving. When the old keeper returned and saw his first creation hopping again after so many years, he could hardly believe his eyes. "You've given me back my first friend," he said, his voice thick with emotion. "You are the finest thing that ever happened to this museum." {~HERO:Nia~} held the little rabbit out to him, and the keeper took it with trembling hands.

{~HERO:Nia~} forced the little lock with the driver, pushing down with all her might. The lock held for a moment. Then, with a sharp crack, the fine old catch broke. The cabinet's door stayed shut, but now it was stuck tight. The broken lock was jammed and would not move. Nothing was harmed that a keeper could not fix, but nothing would open either. {~HERO:Nia~} stepped back, red-faced. She had to accept she would never see the secret inside. She would have to wait and feel a bit silly when she told keeper Fettle she had been too hasty.

The bravest thing might just be to keep the sleeping museum safe. Just let the sky lighten toward grey dawn. Not every problem needed a big fix. Sometimes the best choice was to watch over things and wait. But even so, {~HERO:Nia~} had choices. She could let the animals sleep and wait for morning, doing nothing but keeping watch. She could wind just one loved animal before the light. That would give the museum a single spark of life. Or she could wait by the door to meet whoever came first. She could explain everything she had found. Tock, curled in her lap, seemed content with any of these.

choices.label: Let them sleep and wait for morning.
Wait by the door to meet someone.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Nia~} settled on the floor of the great spring-room with Tock in her lap. The grey light climbed the tall windows, touching the brass fittings and the copper bands of the great silent drum with the first soft glow of morning. The animals slept on, peaceful and still. {~HERO:Nia~} stroked Tock's brass back, feeling his steady ticking under her fingers. It had been a long night, full of wonder and near-misses, and now there was nothing left to do but wait. The dawn felt like a friend arriving at the end of a long journey.

{~HERO:Nia~} kept the whole menagerie safe through the night and watched the sky lighten toward grey dawn. The animals stayed still and sleeping, everything exactly as the keeper had left it. She had not fixed the great spring, but nothing had come to harm either—no gears had fallen, no fragile wings had snapped, no turnstiles had trapped her. When the doors opened, she could tell the keepers all she had learned: where the caretaker master key hung, what had broken, where the spare spring was stored. Some nights, she decided, were for fixing things. And some nights were simply for keeping them safe.

{~HERO:Nia~} thought of all the animals she met during the long night. One in particular had touched her heart. She hurried through the museum with the caretaker master key. The sky outside the high windows turned from grey to pale pink. The animal she chose was waiting for her, still and silent. When she reached it she was sure she had made the right choice. Tock squeaked as she knelt beside it and put the key in its winding socket.

Nia fitted the caretaker master key with care, giving the spring just enough wind to wake for the morning, but saving the rest of its power. This would not be a full winding—just enough to let it stir, to stretch, to greet the dawn. She turned the key four times, each click measured and gentle. Inside the animal, something caught and held. Tock, standing on the nearest surface, leaned forward to watch the magic unfold.

The animal stirred to gentle life under Nia's hands, its mechanisms waking slowly and smoothly. It lifted its head, or spread its wings, or swung on its wires, and in the pale pink light of dawn it was the most beautiful thing Nia had ever seen. She stepped back, pulling Tock with her, and simply watched. She was glad she had chosen it—this one creature, out of all the menagerie, deserved to greet the morning. And so did she.

{~HERO:Nia~} woke one single animal to greet the grey dawn sky. The rest slept on, safe and ready. When the children came, they found one moving wonder among the still ones. It was a lone singer, or a solo dancer, or a gentle giant swaying by the waterhole. It felt like a promise of more wonders to come once keeper Fettle fixed the rest. The children who saw it never forgot that one small waking. {~HERO:Nia~} watched from the clock's shadow and loved the quiet magic of what she had done. Some small joys, she thought, were meant to be kept close.

{~HERO:Nia~} waited by the great front door as the light grew stronger, Tock perched on her shoulder. Soon someone would arrive—the staff, a keeper, or perhaps even an early visitor. She could step forward and meet them openly, explaining everything she had learned. She could leave a helpful note pinned where it couldn't be missed, summarizing the broken spring and the spare in the workshop. Or she could tuck herself out of sight and watch, learning who came before she revealed herself. Each approach had its own kind of wisdom.

choices.label: Leave a helpful note for the morning.
Hide until you know who it is.

nodes.body: {~HERO:Nia~} found a keeper pad on a hook by the door, its pages fresh and a pencil tied to the spine with string. She wrote out everything clearly: the broken great mainspring, the caretaker master key on the hook, the coiled spare mainspring in the workshop, the steps to mend it as drawn in keeper Fettle's manual. When she was done, she read it over twice, then tore the page free. Tock nosed the paper, as if checking it himself. {~HERO:Nia~} pinned it to the wall beside the doorframe, where no one could miss it.

Nia propped the caretaker master key beside the note, leaning it carefully against the wall so that its brass gleam would catch the eye. Anyone who came through that door would see the key first, then the note, and understand. She stepped back, satisfied. Tock squeaked approval. Then Nia found a quiet corner of the rotunda, behind the great museum clock, and settled down to wait. If the keepers needed her, she was here. If they didn't, she would slip out quietly after they had read the note.

The keeper pad told the morning staff just how to mend the great spring. They read {~HERO:Nia~}'s note with growing joy. They found the caretaker master key waiting beside it. In an hour the whole hall was stirring to life. The children who came when the door opened did not know how close the museum had come to a silent day. But {~HERO:Nia~} knew. The keepers were grateful. When they found her dozing behind the clock, they said her clear thinking had saved the morning. One of them told her, "You write a fine set of steps." Tock woke up and preened at the praise.

{~HERO:Nia~} waited by the great front door. At half past seven, the first keeper came. It was a woman with kind eyes and a ring of keys at her belt. She saw {~HERO:Nia~} with Tock and stopped in shock. But she stopped to hear the whole tale. {~HERO:Nia~} told her of the broken spring, the hidden work shop, the master key, and the long night of looking around. The keeper heard it all with great thanks. She saw {~HERO:Nia~} safely home through the waking streets. {~HERO:Nia~} had not mended the hall herself. But she knew she had helped, and that was a fine thing in its own way.

{~HERO:Nia~} hid as the door opened. She ducked behind a case near the front. But the person who came through was only the early cleaner. It was a man with a mop and pail who did not know a child was there. He did his work step by step as he hummed a tune. When he left through the inner gate, he locked it without a glance. The lock clicked shut. {~HERO:Nia~} was still inside. She was safe but stuck. Her chance to tell about the broken spring slipped away. The hall slept through the morning. {~HERO:Nia~} felt a bit silly and had to wait for the cleaner to return and let her out. It was soon put right, but the morning guests found only silent beasts.
